Part 1: Theory
What is a variable?
A variable is a named container that stores a value in memory. You can use that value later in your program and (depending on how it’s declared) update it.
JavaScript has three ways to declare variables:

• var

• let

• const
They differ mainly in:

• Scope (where the variable can be accessed)

• Hoisting behavior (how declarations behave before execution reaches them)

• Re-assignability (whether you can give the variable a new value)
var (legacy, ES5 and earlier)

• Function-scoped (visible throughout the entire function)

• Not block-scoped (it “leaks” out of {} blocks like if/for)

• Hoisted and initialized as undefined

• Can be re-declared and re-assigned

• If declared globally in browsers, it becomes a property on window
let (ES6 / 2015)

• Block-scoped (only visible inside the {} block)

• Hoisted but not initialized (it exists in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) until the declaration line runs)

• Cannot be re-declared in the same scope

• Can be re-assigned
const (ES6 / 2015)

• Block-scoped, like let

• Also has a TDZ

• Cannot be re-declared or re-assigned

• Must be initialized at declaration

• Important nuance: const prevents reassignment of the binding, but objects/arrays can still be mutated

Part 3: Dry Run (step-by-step execution)
Dry running means mentally tracing what happens in memory before and during execution. This is where var, let, and const behave very differently.
Dry Run 1: var hoisting
console.log(a); // ?
var a = 5;
console.log(a); // ?What actually happens (conceptually):
Phase 1 — Memory creation (hoisting):
var a; // hoisted and initialized as undefinedPhase 2 — Execution (line by line):

• console.log(a) → undefined

• a = 5

• console.log(a) → 5
Output:
undefined
5Dry Run 2: let and the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
console.log(b); // ?
let b = 10;
console.log(b); // ?Even though b is hoisted, it’s not initialized until the declaration line runs. Accessing it before that throws:
Output:
ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initializationDry Run 3: Function scope vs block scope
function testVar() {
if (true) {
var x = 1;
}
console.log(x); // ?
}
testVar();function testLet() {
if (true) {
let y = 1;
}
console.log(y); // ?
}
testLet();Output:
1
ReferenceError: y is not definedDry Run 4: var in loops + async callbacks (classic interview gotcha)
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}Output:
3
3
3Why? Because var i is one shared variable; by the time the callbacks run, the loop has finished and i === 3.
Now with let:
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}Output:
0
1
2Because let creates a new binding for each loop iteration.
Dry Run 5: const with objects
const user = { name: "Ali", age: 20 };user.age = 21; // ✅ mutation is allowed
console.log(user); // ?user = { name: "Sara", age: 22 }; // ?Output:
{ name: 'Ali', age: 21 }
TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
Part 4: Interview Questions (with answers)
Q1) What’s the difference between var, let, and const?
Answer: The core differences are:

• Scope: var is function-scoped; let/const are block-scoped.

• Hoisting: var is hoisted and initialized as undefined; let/const are hoisted but live in the TDZ.

• Reassignment: var and let can be reassigned; const cannot.
Q2) What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?
Answer: The TDZ is the time between entering a scope and the point where a let/const declaration is executed. The variable exists but is not accessible; accessing it throws a ReferenceError.
Q3) Predict the output
console.log(x);
var x = 5;Answer: undefined (because var x is hoisted and initialized).
Q4) Predict the output
console.log(y);
let y = 5;Answer: ReferenceError: Cannot access 'y' before initialization (TDZ).
Q5) What will this print?
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100);
}Answer: 3 3 3 (same i shared by all callbacks). Fix by using let or by capturing i in a function scope.
Q6) Can you re-declare a let variable in the same scope?
let a = 1;
let a = 2;Answer: No. This throws SyntaxError: Identifier 'a' has already been declared.
Q7) Is this valid?
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
arr.push(4);Answer: Yes. const prevents reassignment (arr = ...), not mutation (push, editing elements, etc.).
Q8) Why does var attach to the global object but let/const don’t? (browser)
var a = 1;
let b = 2;console.log(window.a); // ?
console.log(window.b); // ?Answer: window.a is 1, but window.b is undefined. Global var becomes a property on the global object; let/const are stored in a separate lexical environment.
Q9) What happens here? (shadowing + block scope)
{
let x = 10;
{
let x = 20;
console.log(x); // ?
}
console.log(x); // ?
}Answer: 20, then 10.
Q10) Why is var considered problematic in modern JS?
Answer: It can leak out of blocks, has confusing hoisting behavior (returns undefined instead of throwing), and often causes bugs in loops with async callbacks.
